brief: TS Lombard's "amber zone" base case (persistent global energy tightness short of a recession-inducing supply crunch) is now "stronger than ever," on a changed basis. The firm had expected amber to rest on the US taking an Iran-Oman deal off-ramp for Strait of Hormuz shipping. Instead, erosion of Iran's blocking capability, per US Energy Secretary Chris Wright's claim that Gulf shipments recovered to 17mbpd (allowing for exaggeration), let Trump declare the "Trump strait" under US control and drop interest in reviving last June's Iran MoU. The new basis is a siege: both sides treat concessions as unacceptable, and since sieges take time, amber looks steady into next year. Mechanics: the US blockade pressures Iran's economy, while high US oil prices sustain midterm "affordability" pressure via retail fuel prices, locked in because "dark" shipping caps Gulf supply at two-thirds of pre-war levels. Each side escalates to force the other to blink, the US via Operation Economic Outcast and Iran via tanker attacks. This week's attacks on two tankers and air-strike exchange fall short of shifting amber to red. Iran's goal is to regain leverage without reblocking, possibly by diverting ships to its own route for revenue, which skews amber toward green.
